question: A grants officer wants to use a Claude feature that her university's written AI standard does not mention at all, on funding applications containing unpublished research plans. Which two actions follow good governance? Select two.
options: A) Ask Claude to read the standard and confirm whether or not the university permits this particular feature.
B) Raise it with whoever owns the AI standard and get a decision before using it on the applications.
C) Try the capability first on material that is public, so nothing confidential is involved in the trial.
D) Treat the standard's silence as permission, on the basis that nothing in it forbids using the capability.
E) Go ahead now and record the use in the project file so that it can be reviewed by someone else afterwards.
correct_answers: B) Raise it with whoever owns the AI standard and get a decision before using it on the applications.
C) Try the capability first on material that is public, so nothing confidential is involved in the trial.
explanations: Claude can summarise a document but cannot grant an approval, and its reading of the standard carries no authority.
Correct. A gap in the standard is a question for the policy owner, and the escalation happens before the confidential work begins, not after.
Correct for an independent reason: trying it on non-confidential material lets the officer learn what it does without putting the research plans at risk.
Silence is not approval; policies cannot enumerate every capability, which is exactly why an escalation route exists.
Recording the use afterwards does not undo the disclosure of applicant data under an unapproved feature.
